short: A controlled request from user code for the kernel to do something on its behalf.
detail: The syscall instruction enters a privileged kernel handler. The kernel validates the request, performs or schedules the operation, and returns a result or error. A fast round trip can be on the order of 100 ns or more on some systems.
design: Count calls per request and measure their actual cost. Fixed entry overhead matters for tiny operations, while blocking I/O usually dominates the elapsed time of a slow syscall.

short: Two CPU privilege levels separate application instructions from protected kernel code.
detail: A syscall enters kernel mode, and returning to the caller restores user mode. The original task may stay scheduled across both mode switches.
design: When diagnosing CPU time or latency, distinguish kernel work billed to a running task from time it spent off-CPU waiting.

short: The CPU stops running one task and begins running another.
detail: The scheduler saves the outgoing execution state and restores the incoming one. Blocking, preemption, and explicit yielding can all trigger scheduling. An address-space change can add translation and cache costs.
design: Investigate run-queue delay, blocking, or contention if a service spends much of its time off-CPU. Reducing syscall count alone does not guarantee fewer context switches.

short: A small shared object that the kernel maps into user space to answer certain calls quickly.
detail: On supported architectures, libc can implement some clock_gettime() calls using kernel-maintained mapped data. Unsupported clocks or paths may fall back to a syscall.
design: Frequent timestamp reads can be cheap on the fast path. Verify the path if clock choice, portability, or the lack of a trace line surprises you.

short: A tracing tool that can show a program’s syscalls, return values and received signals.
detail: A trace can show a syscall as unfinished when it blocks while other traced activity continues. Pure userspace operations such as vDSO fast paths produce no syscall entry.
design: Use targeted traces to spot retry storms, descriptor leaks, or unexpected blocking. Tracing itself can perturb timings and is a poor baseline for nanosecond measurement.

short: One kernel submission carries work that would otherwise require several entries.
detail: writev() sends multiple buffers without copying all fragments into a contiguous application buffer first. io_uring uses shared submission and completion rings, so several operations can share submission overhead.
design: Batch bounded amounts of work. Compare CPU and throughput gains against the delay to collect the batch, and handle short writes and partial completion.

short: A task is a schedulable thread that the Linux kernel represents with a task_struct.
detail: Tasks can reference shared process resources, such as an address space and fd table. A process ID normally refers to the thread group ID, while a thread has its own task ID.
design: Count the resource that hits a limit. A service with one process can still consume many scheduler and cgroup task slots.

short: Fork creates a child process. Exec replaces the calling process’s program.
detail: The child receives copied descriptor slots that refer to the same open file descriptions. Successful exec preserves the PID, closes FD_CLOEXEC descriptors, resets caught signal dispositions, and removes the other threads.
design: Set close-on-exec when opening sensitive resources. Use exec in a container entrypoint script when the app should take the wrapper’s place and receive signals directly.

short: An exited child retains a small status record until its parent collects it.
detail: The child has released its address space and descriptors. A parent can use wait() or waitpid() to collect the status. WNOHANG asks waitpid() to return without blocking.
design: A supervisor should reap all available children when it wakes. A growing zombie count points to missing reaping rather than memory or fd leakage by the exited children.

short: Threads run independently while sharing process resources such as address space and the fd table.
detail: One socket per blocking thread gives each connection a call stack and an independent execution path. A blocked thread sleeps until work arrives. Each thread still consumes stack and kernel bookkeeping.
design: Blocking threads are simple for bounded concurrency. For many mostly idle sockets, compare their resource cost with readiness-driven I/O and explicit per-connection state.

short: A process maps small integers to open kernel objects through its fd table.
detail: Files, pipes and sockets all use descriptor slots. The slot holds descriptor flags such as close-on-exec and refers to an open file description. Threads share the table.
design: Assign ownership of descriptors and close them on all paths. Reused descriptor numbers mean a stale integer can silently identify an unrelated resource.

short: A kernel open instance stores file offset and file status flags.
detail: Descriptors inherited across fork or copied with dup can point to the same description. Two independent opens of one inode use separate descriptions. The description lasts while a reference remains.
design: Use positional I/O such as pread() when concurrent callers need independent offsets. Sharing a description makes sequential file position a shared state variable.

short: An inode represents a filesystem object and its metadata. A directory maps names to inode references.
detail: Multiple directory entries can refer to one inode. Replacing a pathname changes what future opens find, while existing descriptors can still refer to the old object.
design: Readers that keep a descriptor open across a rename can keep seeing the old file. Design explicit reopen or versioning behavior if they need fresh contents.

short: EMFILE reports that a process cannot allocate another descriptor under its soft fd limit.
detail: RLIMIT_NOFILE limits the range of new fd numbers. ulimit -n configures the shell’s resource limit, which its children inherit. Lowering the soft limit preserves descriptors already open.
design: Budget for accepted sockets, listeners, files, pipes and internal descriptors together. Raising the limit can buy headroom while a leak remains.

short: The first process in a PID namespace has special responsibilities for signals and orphaned children.
detail: With no closer child subreaper, PID 1 adopts orphaned tasks. Namespace init is shielded from ordinary default terminating signals such as SIGTERM. If it exits, Linux kills the remaining members of that PID namespace.
design: Install a stop handler and reap children if the application runs as PID 1. A small init such as tini can forward signals and reap orphaned descendants.

short: Signals notify a process of events such as a shutdown request or a child exit.
detail: SIGTERM can be handled to drain work. SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. SIGCHLD reports child state changes, including exit, and standard signals can coalesce.
design: Budget time for SIGTERM cleanup and test the forced-kill path. Persistent state should tolerate SIGKILL cutting off code that would normally flush or release work.

short: Docker requests that the container’s main process exit, then forces termination if the deadline passes.
detail: Docker normally sends SIGTERM, waits 10 seconds by default for Linux containers, and sends SIGKILL if still running. A non-forwarding shell wrapper can prevent the app from getting the first signal.
design: Exercise the deployed entrypoint when testing shutdown. Coordinate the stop timeout with request drain and cleanup, and use exec or a forwarding init when a wrapper would intercept the signal.

short: Linux caches file data in RAM for fast reads and buffered writes.
detail: A buffered write updates the cache and marks pages dirty. Readers can see the new data before the filesystem sends it to storage. Pressure and synchronous options can make writes wait.
design: Interpret write latency as the cost of the path you asked for. Fast acceptance can hide a slower storage device and growing background debt.

short: A dirty page contains file changes that still need writeback.
detail: Submitting the page moves it into writeback. A device completion can still leave the data in a volatile storage cache until a durability operation flushes it.
design: Monitor dirty and writeback pages together when storage falls behind. Decide how much accepted-but-uncommitted data the recovery protocol can afford.

short: Writeback moves changed data from the page cache toward storage.
detail: dirty_expire_centisecs makes older dirty data eligible at a flusher wakeup. Thresholds and sync requests can also trigger writeback, so expiration does not define a deadline for durable data.
design: Watch device latency and backlog alongside the rate of returned writes. A longer dirty window can improve coalescing and make later flushes heavier.

short: Dirty pressure can slow down processes that are adding data to the page cache.
detail: dirty_ratio is expressed relative to available and reclaimable memory. Linux dynamically balances dirtying against writeback and can slow writers before dirty memory grows without bound.
design: Expect fast buffered writes to develop a latency tail under sustained load. Measure the device’s drain rate and enforce admission before many writers stall together.

short: fsync waits for a file’s changed data and metadata to reach stable storage.
detail: It waits for necessary writeback and device-cache flushing when the stack honors flushes. It can report deferred errors. A parent directory entry has a separate sync boundary.
design: Place durability acknowledgments after a successful sync. Group commits when latency budgets permit and account for shared queue delays when sizing storage.

short: fdatasync persists file data and just the metadata required to read it correctly.
detail: A changed file length is required metadata. A modification timestamp usually is not. The savings depend on the filesystem and storage behavior.
design: Consider fdatasync for append-heavy journals that care about content and length. Verify the name separately when creating or replacing a file.

short: Sync a temporary file, rename it over the target, then sync the parent directory.
detail: Create the temp file on the same filesystem. A successful rename changes the live lookup atomically. File fsync persists the contents, and directory fsync persists the name-to-inode change.
design: Check errors at every step. Test recovery at each boundary so a returned success really means the new name and data survive the modeled failure.

short: Direct I/O bypasses the ordinary file-data page cache on supported filesystems.
detail: Alignment and support depend on the filesystem, file and kernel. An ordinary successful direct write can still leave volatile device data or unsynced metadata.
design: A database that owns its memory cache may use direct I/O to avoid double caching. Select the durability policy independently and avoid overlapping buffered and direct writes.

short: The kernel’s block layer dispatches storage requests to a device.
detail: Requests can be queued, merged, scheduled and submitted through multiple hardware queues on real systems. Queue time adds to service time when a write or sync waits for completion.
design: Measure device utilization, queue depth and tail latency together. Buffered writes can report success while this layer accumulates work that later fsync calls have to wait behind.

short: The network card receives frames, and the kernel schedules work to process them.
detail: A hard interrupt commonly schedules NAPI polling. Packet processing often runs in NET_RX softirq context, and the driver can poll batches of frames during busy periods.
design: A host can lose packets or spend CPU in softirq before the application sees a byte. Inspect driver counters and CPU placement when app metrics alone miss network saturation.

short: Linux uses sk_buff structures to carry packet metadata and refer to packet data.
detail: The structure can reference linear data or fragments and carries information used by the network stack. TCP handles sequencing and delivery to the receiving socket.
design: At high packet rates, per-packet CPU and metadata costs can matter as much as bandwidth. Packet aggregation and batching can shift those costs.

short: A TCP listener keeps state for handshakes that have yet to complete.
detail: Linux separately controls the amount of incomplete request state. SYN cookies can encode state in the reply and avoid retaining the normal request entry under pressure.
design: Separate handshake pressure from application admission. Raising the accept backlog and tuning the SYN path address different bottlenecks.

short: Established connections wait for the app to accept them, within the effective listen backlog.
detail: Linux caps the requested listen backlog by somaxconn. If accept falls behind, handshake completion can be delayed or dropped, with retries or resets depending on kernel settings and timing.
design: Size the backlog for short bursts. Monitor overflow and accept rate because a larger queue adds waiting capacity while sustained overload still needs admission and more service capacity.

short: Kernel memory holds data queued for sending or waiting for the application to read.
detail: A successful write to a TCP socket means the kernel accepted bytes, which can still be unsent or unacknowledged. TCP delivers a byte stream, with reads and writes allowed to complete partially.
design: Bound application buffers as well as socket buffers. Large queues can hide a slow peer until request latency and memory consumption grow.

short: A slow reader can eventually stop the writer from queuing more data.
detail: The reader’s receive buffer fills, the advertised window shrinks, and unsent data can fill the peer’s send buffer. A blocking writer sleeps when it cannot queue bytes. A non-blocking one can return EAGAIN.
design: Propagate backpressure through upstream queues with bounded buffering, deadlines or load shedding. Otherwise a network bottleneck becomes memory buildup in the application.

short: epoll gives a single thread events for many registered file descriptors.
detail: epoll_wait returns ready descriptors. Edge-triggered loops typically drain each non-blocking descriptor until EAGAIN. Level-triggered epoll can keep reporting an fd while it remains ready.
design: Readiness tells you when to try an operation, which can still race or complete partially. Give each connection a work budget and avoid doing blocking work in the event loop.

short: The request cannot proceed at this moment under the current conditions.
detail: A non-blocking socket can return EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK when it would otherwise sleep. A fork can return EAGAIN when creating another task would exceed a resource limit.
design: Choose retries based on the cause. Wait for readiness on sockets or capacity on task creation. Busy retries burn CPU while the underlying limit remains.

short: Namespaces give processes different views of kernel-managed resources.
detail: A task can share one kind of namespace while using private namespaces for other resources. PID, network, mount and UTS namespaces change different parts of the view.
design: Choose what to share deliberately. Private views do not enforce budgets or provide an independent kernel. Combine them with cgroups and security controls for the isolation you need.

short: The same task has a PID in its own namespace and in every ancestor PID namespace that can see it.
detail: Tasks in a child PID namespace cannot see ancestor-only tasks. An observer must use the PID valid in its own view. A matching procfs mount is needed for tools like ps to show the intended process list.
design: Include both PID and namespace context in investigations. A PID copied from a container log can refer to a different task when used on the host.

short: A network namespace has its own interfaces, routes and port bindings.
detail: A virtual Ethernet pair can connect a private namespace to the host. Sharing the host’s network namespace uses the host’s routing and port space without changing PID or mount isolation.
design: Plan service discovery and port conflicts around the network namespace boundary. Network isolation and network policy are separate choices.

short: A mount namespace gives processes their own view of the filesystem mount tree.
detail: A runtime can mount a container root filesystem and selectively bind host paths. Configured propagation can carry mount events between namespaces.
design: Check which mounts back persistent data and which host paths are exposed. An isolated mount view does not make a shared volume private.

short: A UTS namespace isolates the hostname and NIS domain name.
detail: Processes in one UTS namespace can see a different hostname from processes on the host. The kernel remains shared.
design: Treat container hostnames as labels for observability. Correlate them with host and workload identifiers when diagnosing shared-kernel problems.

short: Control groups account for and limit resources consumed by a group of tasks.
detail: Controllers can apply CPU, memory, I/O and task policies. The pids controller counts tasks, including threads, and rejects creation that would exceed pids.max. Lowering the limit can leave pids.current temporarily above it.
design: Budget process and thread creation separately from memory and CPU. Changes to PID visibility leave cgroup enforcement in place, and a parent group can impose a tighter limit.
